summary: Describes how to use the ShangMi (SM) cryptographic algorithms with TLS 1.3 and gives a profile for doing so. The IETF does not endorse use of these algorithms; the document exists because they are becoming mandatory in China.

plainLanguage.summary: Some countries require their own secret-code methods. This explains how to use China's with the latest secure web connection.

questions: how do sm2 sm3 sm4 work with tls 1.3
what is the difference between sm4 gcm and ccm
why does china require shangmi algorithms
subtitle: Chinese cryptographic algorithms for secure web connections.

tldr.problem: China is making its own cryptographic algorithms (ShangMi) mandatory, so web security systems need to support them for compatibility and regulatory compliance.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8998 specifies how to use ShangMi algorithms with TLS 1.3: SM2 for digital signatures and key exchange, SM3 as a hash function, and SM4 as the encryption cipher in GCM or CCM modes.
tldr.outcome: Two new cipher suites allow TLS 1.3 connections using ShangMi algorithms, though the IETF does not endorse them. They are an informational specification to support implementation in regions where these algorithms are required.

today: RFC 8998 is an Informational RFC published in March 2021. It remains current as a specification for ShangMi cipher suites in TLS 1.3. The IETF does not endorse these algorithms, but they are mandatory or required in China for government and regulated systems.

sections.title: Introduction to ShangMi Algorithms
sections.content:
The ShangMi (SM) cipher suites bring China's national cryptographic algorithms into TLS 1.3, the latest version of the Transport Layer Security protocol. The RFC defines two new cipher suites: TLS_SM4_GCM_SM3 (with identifier 0x00 0xC6) and TLS_SM4_CCM_SM3 (0x00 0xC7).

Three SM algorithms work together. SM2 is an elliptic curve algorithm used for digital signatures that prove who you are. SM3 is a hash function that produces a 256-bit fingerprint of data. SM4 is a block cipher that encrypts data. The RFC specifies using these instead of the standard RSA, SHA, and AES that most TLS connections use.

The IETF does not endorse these algorithms, but publishes this specification because they are becoming mandatory in China for regulatory compliance. This allows implementers to build compatible systems.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS 1.3 is the system that keeps websites secure. China has its own secret-code methods (SM2, SM3, SM4) that the government requires. This document explains how to use China's methods with TLS 1.3 instead of the usual ones.

sections.title: The ShangMi Algorithms Explained
sections.content:
SM2 is a public-key cryptography scheme based on elliptic curves, standardized in ISO/IEC 14888-3:2018. It uses a fixed 256-bit elliptic curve defined by the Chinese government standard GB/T 32918.5-2017, which means implementations cannot switch to other curves like they can with ECDSA. SM2 handles both digital signatures and the initial key exchange in the TLS handshake.

SM3 is a cryptographic hash function that takes any input and produces a 256-bit output, similar to SHA-256. It is standardized in ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018.

SM4 is a symmetric block cipher that encrypts 16-byte blocks of data, similar to AES. Each block is encrypted using a 16-octet (128-bit) key. It is standardized in ISO/IEC 18033-3:2010.

All three have been accepted into international standards (ISO/IEC) alongside or instead of their Western equivalents, but full security proofs for SM algorithms were not published in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: SM2 is like a personal signature that proves who you are. SM3 is a fingerprint maker that turns any message into a unique short code. SM4 is a lock and key for scrambling messages. Together they replace the RSA, SHA, and AES that most secure websites use.

sections.title: The Two Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The RFC defines exactly two new cipher suites for TLS 1.3. Both use SM4 encryption with SM3 hashing and SM2 signatures, but they differ in how they encrypt data:

TLS_SM4_GCM_SM3 uses SM4 in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM), a widely-used authenticated encryption mode. The SM4 key is 16 octets long, the nonce (starting value) is 12 octets, and the authentication tag is 16 octets. Maximum plaintext length is 2^36 - 31 octets.

TLS_SM4_CCM_SM3 uses SM4 in Counter with CBC-MAC mode (CCM), an alternative authenticated encryption mode. The SM4 key is again 16 octets, the nonce is 12 octets, and the tag is 16 octets. However, CCM limits plaintext to 2^24 - 1 octets per message.

Both modes provide authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD), meaning data is encrypted and integrity-checked in one operation, as required by TLS 1.3. IANA has reserved these identifiers in the TLS Cipher Suites registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds two ways to scramble data using SM4: GCM mode handles much larger messages, while CCM mode handles smaller ones but works differently. Both check that data was not tampered with during delivery.

sections.title: How TLS 1.3 Uses ShangMi
sections.content:
When a TLS 1.3 client and server want to use ShangMi, they negotiate during the handshake. The client's ClientHello message MUST include the new cipher suites, MUST list the SM2 elliptic curve as a supported group, and MUST advertise sm2sig_sm3 as an acceptable signature algorithm.

If the server accepts ShangMi, it puts one of the two SM cipher suites into its ServerHello and responds with a key share for the SM2 curve. During authentication, the server and optionally the client present certificates with SM2 public keys signed by a certificate authority using SM2/SM3. In the CertificateVerify message, they prove they own their private key using an SM2 signature over an SM3 hash of the handshake.

For key derivation, the RFC specifies that implementations MUST follow TLS 1.3 standard key scheduling (from RFC 8446), not a separate SM2 key exchange protocol. This ensures compatibility and security consistency with the base TLS 1.3 specification.
sections.plainLanguage: When two computers want to talk securely using ShangMi, they swap messages during a handshake. They say which SM algorithms they support, prove who they are with SM2 signatures, and then use SM4 to scramble their conversation.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC states that at the time of publication, no known weak keys exist for SM2, SM3, or SM4, and no security issues have been found for these algorithms. The document references published security analyses for GCM (McGrew and Viega) and CCM (Jonsson) modes, both of which are well-studied.

SM2 signatures require an identifier string chosen by the certificate authority. For TLS handshakes (except when verifying peer certificates), implementations MUST use the ASCII string TLSv1.3+GM+Cipher+Suite as the SM2 identifier. When verifying a peer's SM2 certificate, the RFC specifies using the string 1234567812345678 according to GM/T 0009-2012. However, in practice, certificate authorities may use different identifiers, so implementations SHOULD verify this information themselves.

The nonce used in GCM or CCM encryption MUST be unique for each message encrypted with the same key, or GCM's security is destroyed. TLS 1.3 provides a standard method for generating unique nonces.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithms are considered secure as of when the RFC was published. Like all encryption, you must never use the same starting number twice with the same key, or a hacker could spot the pattern.
